topics.title: The alphabet, part 1: α to μ
topics.intro: Ancient Greek uses its own alphabet: 24 letters, many of which you already know from maths and science (π, θ, Δ). Our word “alphabet” is just its first two letters, alpha and beta. Learn twelve now: say each name aloud.
topics.teach: Write your initials in Greek letters and explain which letters you used.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to read the Greek letters in a maths or science textbook.

topics.title: The alphabet, part 2: ν to ω
topics.intro: The second twelve letters, ending with omega, “big o”. Watch for false friends: ρ is r, ν is n, η is e, χ is ch and ω is o. They look like our letters but they are not.
topics.teach: Explain which Greek letters look like English ones but make a different sound.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to write your name in Greek letters.

topics.title: Reading Greek aloud: breathings, diphthongs, accents
topics.intro: Now put the letters together. Every word that starts with a vowel has a breathing: the rough one (ʽ) adds an h, the smooth one (ʼ) adds nothing. Pairs of vowels (diphthongs) make one sound, and the accents show which syllable to stress.
topics.teach: Explain what a rough breathing is, using ἵππος as an example.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to read the names of the Olympian gods aloud in Greek.

topics.title: Words 1: people, gods and war
topics.intro: Fourteen nouns, all from the GCSE vocabulary list, and all masculine words ending -ος. Most have English relatives: knowing λόγος unlocks every “-ology”.
topics.teach: Teach three words and an English word that comes from each.
topics.talk: Play “spot the Greek”: ask {her} to find a Greek root in a science or maths word.

topics.title: Words 2: girls, gifts, battles and days
topics.intro: Fourteen more nouns: feminine words ending -η or -α, and neuter words ending -ον. Nike, the goddess of victory, is hiding in this set.
topics.teach: Explain how you can often tell a noun’s gender from its ending.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what the brand name Nike means in Greek.

topics.title: Words 3: verbs
topics.intro: Fourteen verbs. Greek dictionaries list verbs in the “I” form, so λύω means “I free”. The endings change to show who is doing it.
topics.teach: Teach five verbs and act each one out.
topics.talk: Ask {her} the Greek for “I write” and “I flee”.

topics.title: The article: ὁ, ἡ, τό
topics.intro: Greek has a word for “the” (the article), but none for “a”. The article changes to match its noun in gender, case and number, so it is a great clue to what a noun is doing in the sentence.
topics.teach: Recite the singular article in all three genders.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to chant the article table: ὁ, τόν, τοῦ, τῷ…

topics.title: Nouns: the second declension (λόγος, δῶρον)
topics.intro: In Greek the ending of a noun tells you its job. Nominative: the subject. Accusative: the object. Genitive: “of”. Dative: “to” or “for”. λόγος, λόγον, λόγου, λόγῳ…
topics.teach: Explain the four cases using ὁ ἵππος as the example.
topics.talk: Ask {her} which case the words for “of the god” would be in.

topics.title: Nouns: the first declension (τιμή, χώρα)
topics.intro: Feminine nouns ending -η or -α. The same four cases, different endings: τιμή, τιμήν, τιμῆς, τιμῇ. Words ending -α after ε, ι or ρ keep the α all the way through the singular.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between the τιμή and χώρα patterns.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to decline “the voice” (ἡ φωνή) in the singular.

topics.title: Verbs: the present tense and εἰμί
topics.intro: The ending of a verb tells you who is doing it: λύω (I free), λύεις (you free), λύει (he/she frees), λύομεν, λύετε, λύουσι(ν). “To be” is irregular, as in English: εἰμί, εἶ, ἐστί(ν)…
topics.teach: Chant the present tense of λύω and explain each ending.
topics.talk: Ask {her} the Greek for “we are” and “they are”.

topics.title: Reading sentences
topics.intro: Now read whole sentences. Find the verb first, then the nominative (who does it), then the accusative (to whom). Greek word order is flexible: the endings carry the meaning.
topics.teach: Translate a sentence and explain how you found the subject.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to translate a Greek sentence aloud for you.

topics.title: Prepositions and their cases
topics.intro: Prepositions (in, into, out of, from, towards…) each take a particular case. ἐν takes the dative, εἰς the accusative, ἐκ the genitive. Some change meaning with the case.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ and εἰς τὸν οἶκον.
topics.talk: Ask {her}: which case follows ἐκ, and what does it mean?

topics.title: Adjectives
topics.intro: Adjectives agree with their nouns: καλός, καλή, καλόν. The position of the article matters too: ὁ καλὸς ἵππος is “the beautiful horse”, but ὁ ἵππος καλός is “the horse is beautiful”.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between ὁ σοφὸς στρατηγός and ὁ στρατηγὸς σοφός.
topics.talk: Ask {her} which English words come from καλός and μικρός.

topics.title: The past and the future: imperfect and future tenses
topics.intro: The imperfect (“I was freeing”) adds an augment, ἐ-, to the front: ἔλυον. The future (“I will free”) adds a σ before the ending: λύσω. Spot the clue, then read the ending for the person.
topics.teach: Explain how to tell ἔλυον from λύσω at a glance.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what the augment is.

topics.title: Little words that matter: particles and word order
topics.intro: Greek loves small connecting words: καί, ἀλλά, γάρ, οὖν, μέν… δέ. Some can never come first in a sentence. Spotting them shows how the ideas link.
topics.teach: Explain what μέν… δέ does in a sentence.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to find γάρ in the Theseus story and translate the sentence.

topics.title: Greek inside English
topics.intro: Science, medicine and technology speak Greek: telephone, biology, democracy, dinosaur. Knowing the roots lets you work out words you have never seen before.
topics.teach: Take a long scientific word and break it into its Greek parts.
topics.talk: Pick a word from the news and ask {her} whether it has Greek inside it.

topics.title: Gods, games, theatre and Homer
topics.intro: The language comes with a world: twelve Olympian gods, the first Olympic Games, theatres seating thousands, and Homer’s two great poems, the Iliad and the Odyssey.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between the Iliad and the Odyssey.
topics.talk: Ask {her} which Olympian god {she} would most like to meet, and why.

topics.title: Story: Theseus and the Minotaur
topics.intro: A whole story in Greek, using words you know plus a glossary. Read it twice, aloud if you can. Theseus, prince of Athens, goes into the labyrinth.
topics.teach: Retell the story in English, then translate your favourite sentence.
topics.talk: Ask {her} to read a sentence of the story aloud in Greek and translate it.

topics.title: Stories: Odysseus and the Cyclops, Perseus and Medusa
topics.intro: Two more adapted myths: Odysseus tricks the Cyclops with a famous pun, and Perseus faces Medusa with help from two gods.
topics.teach: Explain the joke in Odysseus’ false name.
topics.talk: Ask {her} why the other Cyclopes did not come to help.

topics.title: The aorist: “I freed”
topics.intro: The aorist is the most common past tense in stories: a single completed action. The weak aorist adds an augment and -σα: ἔλυσα, “I freed”. Some common verbs have strong aorists you just learn: ἔφυγον, “I fled”.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between ἔλυον and ἔλυσα.
topics.talk: Ask {her} the aorist of λύω and what it means.

topics.title: The third declension: a taster
topics.intro: The third declension is the big, varied family: φύλαξ (guard), ὄνομα (name), ἀνήρ (man), πόλις (city). Find the stem from the genitive, then add the endings.
topics.teach: Explain why you need the genitive to decline φύλαξ.
topics.talk: Ask {her} which English words come from πόλις and ὄνομα.

topics.title: Participles: a taster
topics.intro: A participle is a verb used as an adjective: λύων means “freeing”. Greek uses them everywhere, often where English would use “who”, “while” or “after”.
topics.teach: Translate ὁ φεύγων στρατηγός two different ways.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what ὁ λύων means.

ἐν + dative = in, on: ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ = in the house.
εἰς + accusative = into, to: εἰς τὸν ποταμόν = into the river.
ἐκ (ἐξ before a vowel) + genitive = out of: ἐκ τῆς χώρας = out of the land.
ἀπό + genitive = from, away from: ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγορᾶς = from the market place.
πρός + accusative = towards, to: πρὸς τὸν στρατηγόν = towards the general.
μετά + genitive = with: μετὰ τῶν φίλων = with the friends.
μετά + accusative = after: μετὰ τὴν μάχην = after the battle.
διά + accusative = because of: διὰ τὸν πόλεμον = because of the war.
διά + genitive = through: διὰ τῆς χώρας = through the land.
A neat pattern: being IN a place = dative; motion INTO = accusative; motion OUT OF = genitive.
εἰς τὴν Κρήτην = into Crete, to Crete.

items.passage:
ὁ Θησεὺς καὶ ὁ Μινώταυρος

ἐν τῇ Κρήτῃ ὁ Μίνως βασιλεύει. ἐν δὲ τῷ λαβυρίνθῳ μένει ὁ Μινώταυρος· δεινὸς γάρ ἐστιν. οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι ἑπτὰ νεανίας καὶ ἑπτὰ κόρας εἰς τὴν Κρήτην πέμπουσιν. ὁ δὲ Θησεὺς ἀνδρεῖός ἐστιν· ἐθέλει οὖν τοὺς φίλους λύειν.

ἡ Ἀριάδνη, ἡ τοῦ βασιλέως θυγάτηρ, τὸν Θησέα φιλεῖ καὶ λίνον αὐτῷ δίδωσιν. ὁ Θησεὺς εἰς τὸν λαβύρινθον βαίνει καὶ τὸν Μινώταυρον ἀποκτείνει. ἔπειτα τῷ λίνῳ τὴν ὁδὸν εὑρίσκει καὶ ἐκ τοῦ λαβυρίνθου φεύγει. οἱ οὖν Ἀθηναῖοι μάλα χαίρουσιν.

Glossary: βασιλεύει = is king; λαβύρινθος = labyrinth, maze; νεανίας (accusative plural νεανίας) = young man; θυγάτηρ = daughter; φιλεῖ = loves; λίνον = thread; αὐτῷ = to him; δίδωσιν = gives; βαίνει = goes; ἀποκτείνει = kills; ἔπειτα = then; ὁδός (accusative ὁδόν) = way, road; εὑρίσκει = finds; μάλα = very much; χαίρουσιν = rejoice.

items.passage:
ὁ Θησεὺς καὶ ὁ Μινώταυρος

ἐν τῇ Κρήτῃ ὁ Μίνως βασιλεύει. ἐν δὲ τῷ λαβυρίνθῳ μένει ὁ Μινώταυρος· δεινὸς γάρ ἐστιν. οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι ἑπτὰ νεανίας καὶ ἑπτὰ κόρας εἰς τὴν Κρήτην πέμπουσιν. ὁ δὲ Θησεὺς ἀνδρεῖός ἐστιν· ἐθέλει οὖν τοὺς φίλους λύειν.

ἡ Ἀριάδνη, ἡ τοῦ βασιλέως θυγάτηρ, τὸν Θησέα φιλεῖ καὶ λίνον αὐτῷ δίδωσιν. ὁ Θησεὺς εἰς τὸν λαβύρινθον βαίνει καὶ τὸν Μινώταυρον ἀποκτείνει. ἔπειτα τῷ λίνῳ τὴν ὁδὸν εὑρίσκει καὶ ἐκ τοῦ λαβυρίνθου φεύγει. οἱ οὖν Ἀθηναῖοι μάλα χαίρουσιν.

items.passage:
ὁ Ὀδυσσεὺς καὶ ὁ Κύκλωψ

ὁ Ὀδυσσεὺς καὶ οἱ φίλοι ἐκ τῆς Τροίας οἴκαδε πλέουσιν. ἐν νήσῳ ἄντρον εὑρίσκουσιν. ἐν δὲ τῷ ἄντρῳ μένει ὁ Πολύφημος, Κύκλωψ δεινὸς καὶ μέγιστος. ὁ Κύκλωψ τοὺς φίλους ἐσθίει.

ὁ δὲ Ὀδυσσεὺς σοφός ἐστιν. τῷ Κύκλωπι οἶνον δίδωσι καὶ λέγει· «Οὖτις ὄνομά μοί ἐστιν.» ὁ Κύκλωψ τὸν οἶνον πίνει καὶ καθεύδει. ἔπειτα ὁ Ὀδυσσεὺς καὶ οἱ φίλοι τὸν Κύκλωπα τυφλοῦσιν.

ὁ Πολύφημος βοᾷ· «Οὖτίς με ἀποκτείνει.» οἱ οὖν ἄλλοι Κύκλωπες οὐ βοηθοῦσιν. ὁ δὲ Ὀδυσσεὺς καὶ οἱ φίλοι ὑπὸ τοῖς προβάτοις ἐκ τοῦ ἄντρου φεύγουσιν.

ὁ Ὀδυσσεὺς καὶ οἱ φίλοι ἐκ τῆς Τροίας οἴκαδε πλέουσιν. ἐν νήσῳ ἄντρον εὑρίσκουσιν. ἐν δὲ τῷ ἄντρῳ μένει ὁ Πολύφημος, Κύκλωψ δεινὸς καὶ μέγιστος. ὁ Κύκλωψ τοὺς φίλους ἐσθίει.

ὁ δὲ Ὀδυσσεὺς σοφός ἐστιν. τῷ Κύκλωπι οἶνον δίδωσι καὶ λέγει· «Οὖτις ὄνομά μοί ἐστιν.» ὁ Κύκλωψ τὸν οἶνον πίνει καὶ καθεύδει. ἔπειτα ὁ Ὀδυσσεὺς καὶ οἱ φίλοι τὸν Κύκλωπα τυφλοῦσιν.

ὁ Πολύφημος βοᾷ· «Οὖτίς με ἀποκτείνει.» οἱ οὖν ἄλλοι Κύκλωπες οὐ βοηθοῦσιν. ὁ δὲ Ὀδυσσεὺς καὶ οἱ φίλοι ὑπὸ τοῖς προβάτοις ἐκ τοῦ ἄντρου φεύγουσιν.

items.passage:
ὁ Περσεὺς καὶ ἡ Μέδουσα

ἡ Μέδουσα Γοργώ ἐστιν· οἱ ἄνθρωποι, εἰ αὐτὴν βλέπουσιν, λίθοι γίγνονται. ὁ δὲ Περσεὺς τὴν Μέδουσαν ἀποκτείνειν ἐθέλει.

ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ τῷ Περσεῖ ἀσπίδα λαμπρὰν δίδωσιν, ὁ δὲ Ἑρμῆς πτερωτὰ πέδιλα. ὁ Περσεὺς οὐ βλέπει τὴν Μέδουσαν, ἀλλὰ τὴν εἰκόνα ἐν τῇ ἀσπίδι. οὕτω τὴν κεφαλὴν ἀποτέμνει καὶ ἐκ τῆς χώρας φεύγει.

Glossary: Γοργώ = a Gorgon; εἰ = if; αὐτήν = her; βλέπουσιν = look at; λίθοι = stones; γίγνονται = become; ἀποκτείνειν = to kill; ἀσπίς (accusative ἀσπίδα, dative ἀσπίδι) = shield; λαμπρός = bright, shining; πτερωτὰ πέδιλα = winged sandals; εἰκών (accusative εἰκόνα) = image, reflection; οὕτω = in this way; κεφαλή = head; ἀποτέμνει = cuts off.

items.prompt: What does the aorist usually describe?

options.text: A single, completed action in the past
An action that kept going on in the past

items.explain: ἔλυον = I was freeing; ἔλυσα = I freed (once, done).
Augment ἐ- + stem λυ + σα: the weak aorist, “I freed”.

items.prompt: Which is the aorist of λύω for “they freed”?

options.feedback: ἔλυον is imperfect: they were freeing.
λύσουσι(ν) is future: they will free.

items.explain: ἔλυσα, ἔλυσας, ἔλυσε(ν), ἐλύσαμεν, ἐλύσατε, ἔλυσαν.

options.feedback: The σε shows the aorist, not the imperfect (ἐπαίδευε).

items.explain: ἐ- (augment) + παιδευ + σε: he/she taught.

items.prompt: The aorist of πέμπω is ἔπεμψα. What does it mean?

options.feedback: The augment shows it is past.

items.explain: π + σ → ψ, just like the future πέμψω, but with the augment: ἔπεμψα.

items.prompt: Some verbs have a “strong” aorist with a different stem. The aorist of φεύγω (I flee) is ἔφυγον. What does it mean?

options.feedback: That is ἔφευγον, the imperfect. Note the stem change: φευγ → φυγ.
The augment shows it is past.

items.explain: Strong aorists have imperfect-style endings on a different stem: ἔφυγον, ἔλαβον (I took), εἶπον (I said).

items.prompt: εἶπον is the aorist of which verb?

options.feedback: The aorist of ἔχω is ἔσχον.
The aorist of πέμπω is ἔπεμψα.

items.explain: Some aorists have to be learned as new words: λέγω → εἶπον.

items.prompt: The genitive of φύλαξ (guard) is φύλακος. What is its stem?

options.feedback: The ξ in the nominative hides κ + σ. The genitive shows the true stem.
Take the genitive and remove -ος: φυλακ-.

items.explain: Third-declension rule: find the stem by removing -ος from the genitive. φύλαξ, φύλακα, φύλακος, φύλακι.

items.prompt: What is the accusative singular of **φύλαξ**?

options.feedback: -ον is second declension. Third-declension accusatives end -α.

items.explain: φύλαξ, φύλακα, φύλακος, φύλακι.

items.prompt: ὄνομα (name) has genitive ὀνόματος. Which English words come from it?

options.feedback: Those have nothing to do with ὄνομα.

items.explain: ἀν- (without) + ὄνομα = anonymous; ὀνοματοποιία = “name-making”.

options.text: the man (a grown man, or a husband)

options.feedback: That is ὁ ἄνθρωπος. ἀνήρ is a man, a husband.

items.explain: ἀνήρ, ἄνδρα, ἀνδρός, ἀνδρί: gives us Andrew and android (“man-like”).

items.prompt: What does **ἡ πόλις** mean, and which English words come from it?

options.feedback: Pole comes from a different Greek word, πόλος (axis).

items.explain: πόλις, πόλιν, πόλεως, πόλει. μητρόπολις = “mother city”.

items.prompt: Which ending marks the dative singular in the third declension?
items.explain: Third declension singular: (nominative varies), -α, -ος, -ι.

options.text: the one who frees, the man freeing

options.feedback: λύων is a verb form (freeing), not the adjective “free”.

items.explain: A participle with the article = “the one who…”: ὁ λύων, ὁ γράφων, ὁ φεύγων.

items.prompt: Best translation of **ὁ στρατηγὸς φεύγων τὸν ποταμὸν ὁρᾷ**?

options.text: While fleeing, the general sees the river

options.feedback: φεύγων is a participle (fleeing); the main verb is ὁρᾷ, sees.

options.text: The general sees the fleeing river
options.feedback: φεύγων agrees with ὁ στρατηγός (nominative), not with the river.

items.explain: A present participle often becomes “while…” or “as…” in English.

items.prompt: λύων, λύουσα, λῦον are the masculine, feminine and neuter of the present participle. Which goes with ἡ κόρη?
items.explain: Participles agree like adjectives: ἡ κόρη ἡ λύουσα = the girl who is freeing.

items.prompt: λύσας is the aorist participle of λύω. What does **ὁ Θησεὺς τοὺς φίλους λύσας φεύγει** mean?

options.text: Having freed his friends, Theseus flees
While freeing his friends, Theseus flees
options.feedback: The aorist participle usually means “having…” or “after…”.
λύσας (having freed) is the participle; φεύγει is the main verb.

items.explain: Aorist participle = an action completed before the main verb: “having freed”, “after freeing”.
